3.2.1.examLens: Build a confidence interval by hand, read the t table correctly, and know what a confidence interval does and does not mean.

worked.question: A sample of 10 cycle times has mean 24.0 minutes and s = 3.0. (a) Build a 95% confidence interval for the mean. (b) How large a sample would roughly halve the interval width?
worked.solution:
(a) SE = 3.0 ÷ √10 = 0.949. df = 9, two-tailed 95% uses the 0.975 column: t = 2.262. Margin = 2.262 × 0.949 = 2.15. Interval = 21.85 to 26.15 minutes.
(b) Halving the width needs about four times the sample, so roughly 40.

3.2.2.examLens: Identify the sampling method from a description, and compute a sample size for a mean or a proportion. For hypothesis tests, know what drives the sample size.

worked.question: (a) A quality manager inspects every 20th unit off a conveyor. Which method? (b) How many units are needed to estimate a mean within ±2 if σ = 10 and confidence is 95%? (c) A proportion with no prior estimate, margin ±0.03, 95% confidence?

3.2.3.examLens: Compute the standard error of a mean and probabilities for a sample mean, and avoid using σ where you should use σ/√n.

worked.question: A process has μ = 50 and σ = 6. Samples of n = 36 are taken. (a) What is the standard error? (b) What is the probability a sample mean exceeds 52? (c) If n is increased to 144, what happens to the standard error?
worked.solution:
(a) SE = 6 ÷ 6 = 1.
(b) z = (52 − 50) ÷ 1 = 2.0, right tail = 0.0228.
(c) SE = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5. Quadrupling n halves the standard error.

3.2.1.a.title: What inference is
3.2.1.a.html: Inference means drawing conclusions about a population from a sample. You cannot measure everything, so you measure part and use statistics to say what the whole is likely to be.

3.2.1.b.title: Point estimate versus interval estimate
3.2.1.b.html:
• A point estimate is a single number (the sample mean x̄).
  • An interval estimate is a range likely to contain the true value (a confidence interval). It shows how much uncertainty surrounds the estimate.

3.2.1.c.title: Confidence interval for a mean
3.2.1.c.html:
x̄ ± t(α/2, n − 1) × s ÷ √n.
Example: n = 16, x̄ = 50, s = 8. Standard error = 8 ÷ 4 = 2. For 95% confidence with df = 15, t = 2.131. Margin = 2.131 × 2 = 4.26. Interval = 45.7 to 54.3.

3.2.1.d.title: Standard error
3.2.1.d.html: SE = s ÷ √n. It measures how much the sample mean varies from sample to sample.

3.2.1.e.title: What makes the interval wider or narrower
3.2.1.e.html:
• Larger n: narrower.
  • Higher confidence level (99% versus 95%): wider.
  • More variation (larger s): wider.

3.2.1.f.title: What "95% confidence" means
3.2.1.f.html: If you repeated the sampling many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true value. It is not correct to say "there is a 95% chance this particular interval contains the true mean."

3.2.1.g.title: z or t?
3.2.1.g.html: Use z when the population σ is known. Use t when σ is estimated from the sample (the usual case).

3.2.1.h.title: Degrees of freedom
3.2.1.h.html: For a single sample, df = n − 1. One degree of freedom is "used up" estimating the mean. Smaller samples have smaller df and wider t-values.

3.2.1.i.title: Which change narrows the interval?
3.2.1.i.html: Increase the sample size. Because SE contains √n, you need four times the data to cut the width in half.

3.2.1.j.title: Confidence interval for a proportion
3.2.1.j.html:
p̂ ± z × √[ p̂(1 − p̂) ÷ n ].
Example: 18 defective in 200. p̂ = 0.09. SE = √(0.09 × 0.91 ÷ 200) = 0.0202. Margin = 1.96 × 0.0202 = 0.040. Interval = 5.0% to 13.0%.

3.2.1.k.title: Reading the t table
3.2.1.k.html:
The t table in the exam reference document works like this:

  • Table 1 columns are cumulative probabilities, 0.600 to 0.995. The header says "Alpha Risk," but the values are really 1 − α. Table 2 shows the same critical values to more decimals, with columns labeled by one-tail α (0.25, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.01, 0.005).
  • Rows are df = n − 1: 1 to 30, then 40, 60, 120, and ∞.
  • Two-tailed α = 0.05 uses the 0.975 column of Table 1 (or the 0.025 column of Table 2). One-tailed α = 0.05 uses the 0.950 column (or the 0.05 column of Table 2).
  • If your df is not listed, use the next lower listed df (it is conservative).

Examples: df = 9, 0.975 column: 2.262. df = 9, 0.950 column: 1.833. df = 35 is not listed, so use df = 30: 2.042.

3.2.2.a.title: The methods
3.2.2.a.html:
• Simple random: every unit has an equal chance of being chosen.
  • Stratified: divide the population into groups (strata), then sample from each.
  • Systematic: take every k-th unit.
  • Cluster: randomly choose whole groups (clusters), then measure everything in them.
  • Convenience: whatever is easy to reach. Prone to bias.
  • Judgment: the sampler chooses what they think is representative.

3.2.2.b.title: When to use which
3.2.2.b.html: Use stratified sampling when the population has distinct subgroups (shifts, machines, suppliers) you want represented. Use systematic sampling for steady line-based sampling (every 10th unit).

3.2.2.c.title: Sample size for a mean
3.2.2.c.html:
n = (Z(α/2) × σ ÷ E)², where E is the margin of error you can tolerate.
Example: σ = 12, E = 3, 95% confidence. n = (1.96 × 12 ÷ 3)² = 7.84² = 61.5, so round up to 62.

3.2.2.d.title: Sample size for a proportion
3.2.2.d.html:
n = Z² × p(1 − p) ÷ E². If you have no estimate for p, use p = 0.5, which gives the largest (safest) n.
Example: E = 0.05, 95% confidence, p = 0.5. n = 3.8416 × 0.25 ÷ 0.0025 = 384.2, so round up to 385.

3.2.2.e.title: What drives sample size
3.2.2.e.html: Sample size depends on the confidence level (α), the power you want, the variation (σ), and the smallest difference worth detecting.

3.2.2.f.title: Sampling bias
3.2.2.f.html:
• Selection bias: the way units are picked favors some over others.
  • Non-response bias: the people who respond differ from those who do not.
  • Undercoverage: part of the population is left out of the list you sample from.

3.2.2.g.title: Name the method from the description
3.2.2.g.html: "Every 10th unit off the line" is systematic. "Pick five units from each of the three shifts" is stratified. "Randomly choose two plants and inspect every unit there" is cluster.

3.2.2.h.title: Two kinds of sample size
3.2.2.h.html:
• Precision (for an estimate): how tight do you want the interval? (Formulas above.)
  • Power (for a hypothesis test): how likely do you want to detect a real difference? This needs α, power, σ, and the smallest difference worth detecting.

3.2.2.i.title: Sample size for a hypothesis test
3.2.2.i.html:
• 1-sample t: n ≈ (Z(α/2) + Z(β))² × σ² ÷ δ².
  • 2-sample t, equal n per group: n ≈ 2 × (Z(α/2) + Z(β))² × σ² ÷ δ².

Here δ is the smallest difference worth detecting and Z(β) goes with the power you want. n rises with σ and power, and falls with δ and α.
Example: σ = 4, δ = 2, α = 0.05 two-sided (Z = 1.96), power 0.90 (Z(β) = 1.28 from the Z table). (1.96 + 1.28)² = 10.50. 1-sample: 10.50 × 16 ÷ 4 = 42. 2-sample: 2 × 10.50 × 16 ÷ 4 = 84 per group.

3.2.3.a.title: The statement
3.2.3.a.html: As the sample size increases, the distribution of sample means becomes approximately normal, regardless of the shape of the population the data come from.

3.2.3.b.title: Mean and standard error
3.2.3.b.html:
• The mean of the sample means equals the population mean μ.
  • The standard deviation of the sample means (the standard error) is σ ÷ √n.

3.2.3.c.title: How large is large enough?
3.2.3.c.html: n of 30 or more is a classroom rule of thumb. The sample size you actually need depends on how skewed the population is, how heavy its tails are, and whether there are outliers.

3.2.3.d.title: Why it matters
3.2.3.d.html: This is why Xbar charts and t-tests for means work reasonably well even when individual values are not normal: they are built on averages.

3.2.3.e.title: What it does not do
3.2.3.e.html: The CLT does not make individual values normal. It is a statement about averages.

3.2.3.f.title: Probabilities for a sample mean
3.2.3.f.html:
Use the standard error in the z-score: z = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ ÷ √n).
Example: μ = 100, σ = 10, n = 25. SE = 10 ÷ 5 = 2. P(x̄ above 103): z = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5, right tail = 0.0668. Compare an individual value above 103 (assuming normal data): z = 0.3, tail = 0.382.

3.2.3.g.title: σ versus standard error
3.2.3.g.html: With σ = 10 and n = 25, the standard error is 2, not 10. Using σ when the question is about a sample mean is the most common mistake.

3.2.1-1.stem: A sample of 25 values has a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 10. Which is the 95% confidence interval for the population mean?
3.2.1-1.explanation: SE = 10 ÷ 5 = 2. For df = 24, the two-tailed 95% value is t = 2.064. Margin = 2.064 × 2 = 4.13. Interval = 35.9 to 44.1.

3.2.1-2.stem: Which is the correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval?

options.html: There is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains the true mean
If the sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true mean
95% of individual values fall inside the interval
The sample mean is correct 95% of the time

3.2.1-2.explanation: Confidence describes the long-run performance of the method, not the probability for one fixed interval.

3.2.1-3.stem: Which single change would narrow a confidence interval for a mean?

options.html: Increase the confidence level from 95% to 99%

3.2.1-3.explanation: A larger sample reduces the standard error. A higher confidence level or more variation widens the interval.

3.2.1-4.stem: For a sample of 12, what t value would you read from the Reference Document for a two-sided 95% interval?
3.2.1-4.explanation: df = 11. The 0.975 column of Table 1 (or the 0.025 column of Table 2) gives 2.201.

3.2.1-5.stem: A sample finds 18 defective units out of 200. Which is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the defective proportion?

3.2.1-6.stem: When the population standard deviation is estimated from the sample, a t distribution is used for inference about the mean.
3.2.1-6.explanation: Use z only when σ is known. In practice σ is estimated, so t is used.

3.2.2-1.stem: A quality manager picks 5 units from each of the three shifts. Which sampling method is this?
3.2.2-1.explanation: The population is split into groups (shifts) and sampled within each group, which is stratified sampling.

3.2.2-2.stem: An inspector pulls every 20th unit off a conveyor. Which sampling method is this?
3.2.2-2.explanation: Taking every k-th unit is systematic sampling.

options.html: The experience of the Black Belt

3.2.2-5.explanation: Sample size depends on α, power, the variation (σ), and the smallest difference worth detecting.

3.2.2-6.stem: A team wants to detect a difference of 2 between two means. The standard deviation is 4, α = 0.05 (two-sided, Z = 1.96), and power is 0.90 (Z = 1.28). Using equal groups, about how many observations are needed in each group?

3.2.3-1.stem: A process has σ = 12. What is the standard error of the mean for samples of n = 36?
3.2.3-1.explanation: SE = σ ÷ √n = 12 ÷ 6 = 2. Using σ itself (12) is the common error.

3.2.3-2.stem: For a process with μ = 50 and σ = 12, what is the probability that a sample mean of n = 36 exceeds 53?

3.2.3-3.stem: The Central Limit Theorem makes individual data values follow a normal distribution when the sample is large.
3.2.3-3.explanation: The CLT is about the distribution of sample means, not of individual values.

3.2.3-4.stem: If the sample size is quadrupled, what happens to the standard error of the mean?

options.html: It is cut to a quarter

3.2.3-4.explanation: SE = σ ÷ √n, so quadrupling n divides SE by 2.
